# What is NestJS?

NestJS is a framework for building efficient, scalable Node.js server-side applications. It uses progressive JavaScript, is built with and fully supports TypeScript, and combines elements of OOP, FP, and FRP. Under the hood, Nest makes use of robust HTTP server frameworks like Express (the default) and optionally can be configured to use Fastify.

subtopics.content:
# NestJS vs Express

Express is a minimal, unopinionated Node.js framework that gives developers full control but requires manual setup of architecture, validation, and other concerns. NestJS, built on top of Express (or Fastify), provides a structured, opinionated architecture with built-in dependency injection, modules, and decorators. NestJS is better for large-scale applications, while Express excels in simple, lightweight APIs.

subtopics.name: installation-and-setup
subtopics.title: Installation & Setup
subtopics.description: Setting up a NestJS project involves installing the Nest CLI globally via npm and using it to scaffold a new project. The CLI generates a well-structured project with TypeScript configuration, ESLint, testing setup (Jest), and a basic module/controller/service structure. subtopics.content:
# Installation & Setup

Setting up a NestJS project involves installing the Nest CLI globally via npm and using it to scaffold a new project. The CLI generates a well-structured project with TypeScript configuration, ESLint, testing setup (Jest), and a basic module/controller/service structure. modules.title: Core Concepts
modules.description: NestJS is built around three core building blocks: Modules, Controllers, and Providers (Services). Modules organize the application into cohesive blocks, Controllers handle incoming requests and return responses, and Providers (Services) contain the business logic. Understanding Dependency Injection and how NestJS uses Decorators is fundamental to building any NestJS application.

subtopics.name: modules
subtopics.title: Modules
subtopics.description: A module is a class annotated with a @Module() decorator. The @Module() decorator provides metadata that Nest uses to organize the application structure. Each application has at least one module, a root module. Modules are strongly recommended as an effective way to organize components, encapsulating providers and controllers into cohesive blocks of functionality.
subtopics.content:
# Modules

A module is a class annotated with a @Module() decorator. The @Module() decorator provides metadata that Nest uses to organize the application structure. Each application has at least one module, a root module. Modules are strongly recommended as an effective way to organize components, encapsulating providers and controllers into cohesive blocks of functionality.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: controllers
subtopics.title: Controllers
subtopics.description: Controllers are responsible for handling incoming requests and returning responses to the client. A controller's purpose is to receive specific requests for the application. The routing mechanism controls which controller receives which requests. Controllers are defined using the @Controller() decorator and contain route handlers decorated with HTTP method decorators like @Get(), @Post(), @Put(), @Delete().
subtopics.content:
# Controllers

Controllers are responsible for handling incoming requests and returning responses to the client. A controller's purpose is to receive specific requests for the application. The routing mechanism controls which controller receives which requests. Controllers are defined using the @Controller() decorator and contain route handlers decorated with HTTP method decorators like @Get(), @Post(), @Put(), @Delete().

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: providers-and-services
subtopics.title: Providers & Services
subtopics.description: Providers are a fundamental concept in Nest. Many of the basic Nest classes may be treated as a provider — services, repositories, factories, helpers, and so on. The main idea of a provider is that it can be injected as a dependency. Services are the most common type of provider, containing the business logic that is used by controllers.
subtopics.content:
# Providers & Services

Providers are a fundamental concept in Nest. Many of the basic Nest classes may be treated as a provider — services, repositories, factories, helpers, and so on. The main idea of a provider is that it can be injected as a dependency. Services are the most common type of provider, containing the business logic that is used by controllers.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: dependency-injection
subtopics.title: Dependency Injection
subtopics.description: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern in which a class receives its dependencies from external sources rather than creating them itself. NestJS has a built-in IoC (Inversion of Control) container that resolves dependencies between providers. By using the @Injectable() decorator and constructor injection, NestJS manages the lifecycle and scope of providers automatically.
subtopics.content:
# Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern in which a class receives its dependencies from external sources rather than creating them itself. NestJS has a built-in IoC (Inversion of Control) container that resolves dependencies between providers. By using the @Injectable() decorator and constructor injection, NestJS manages the lifecycle and scope of providers automatically.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: decorators
subtopics.title: Decorators
subtopics.description: Decorators are a core language feature used extensively in NestJS. They are special expressions that attach metadata to classes, methods, or parameters. NestJS provides many built-in decorators (@Controller, @Get, @Post, @Injectable, @Body, @Param, @Query, etc.) and allows creating custom decorators using createParamDecorator() for reusable request logic.
subtopics.content:
# Decorators

Decorators are a core language feature used extensively in NestJS. They are special expressions that attach metadata to classes, methods, or parameters. NestJS provides many built-in decorators (@Controller, @Get, @Post, @Injectable, @Body, @Param, @Query, etc.) and allows creating custom decorators using createParamDecorator() for reusable request logic.

modules.title: TypeScript Basics for NestJS
modules.description: NestJS is built with and fully supports TypeScript. Understanding TypeScript fundamentals — including interfaces, types, enums, classes, generics, and basic OOP principles — is essential for working effectively with NestJS. TypeScript's static type system helps catch errors at compile time and improves developer experience with better IDE support.

subtopics.name: interfaces-and-types
subtopics.title: Interfaces & Types
subtopics.description: TypeScript interfaces and type aliases define the shape of objects, enabling type checking and IDE autocompletion. In NestJS, interfaces are commonly used to define DTOs (Data Transfer Objects), entity shapes, and service contracts. Understanding the differences between interface and type, and when to use each, is crucial for writing clean NestJS code.
subtopics.content:
# Interfaces & Types

TypeScript interfaces and type aliases define the shape of objects, enabling type checking and IDE autocompletion. In NestJS, interfaces are commonly used to define DTOs (Data Transfer Objects), entity shapes, and service contracts. Understanding the differences between interface and type, and when to use each, is crucial for writing clean NestJS code.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: enums
subtopics.title: Enums
subtopics.description: Enums allow defining a set of named constants. In NestJS applications, enums are commonly used for user roles, status codes, configuration options, and any value with a fixed set of options. TypeScript supports both numeric and string enums, with string enums being more readable and debuggable.
subtopics.content:
# Enums

Enums allow defining a set of named constants. In NestJS applications, enums are commonly used for user roles, status codes, configuration options, and any value with a fixed set of options. TypeScript supports both numeric and string enums, with string enums being more readable and debuggable.

Understanding OOP fundamentals like encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism is key to mastering NestJS.

modules.title: Building REST APIs
modules.description: Building REST APIs is one of the primary use cases for NestJS. Using decorators like @Controller(), @Get(), @Post(), @Put(), @Delete(), NestJS provides an elegant way to define routes and handle HTTP requests. Understanding request payloads, query parameters, route parameters, and DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) is essential for building robust APIs.

subtopics.name: route-decorators
subtopics.title: Route Decorators (@Get, @Post, @Put, @Delete)
subtopics.description: NestJS uses HTTP method decorators to define route handlers. @Get(), @Post(), @Put(), @Patch(), @Delete() map to the corresponding HTTP methods. These decorators can accept a path string for sub-routing. Route parameters can be defined using :param syntax and accessed via @Param() decorator.
subtopics.content:
# Route Decorators (@Get, @Post, @Put, @Delete)

NestJS uses HTTP method decorators to define route handlers. @Get(), @Post(), @Put(), @Patch(), @Delete() map to the corresponding HTTP methods. These decorators can accept a path string for sub-routing. Route parameters can be defined using :param syntax and accessed via @Param() decorator.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: request-payloads-and-dtos
subtopics.title: Request Payloads & DTOs
subtopics.description: DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) define the shape of data sent in requests. In NestJS, DTOs are TypeScript classes that describe the expected structure of request bodies, query parameters, and route parameters. Using @Body(), @Param(), @Query(), and @Headers() decorators, controllers extract data from incoming requests. DTOs combined with validation pipes ensure type safety and data integrity.
subtopics.content:
# Request Payloads & DTOs

DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) define the shape of data sent in requests. In NestJS, DTOs are TypeScript classes that describe the expected structure of request bodies, query parameters, and route parameters. Using @Body(), @Param(), @Query(), and @Headers() decorators, controllers extract data from incoming requests. DTOs combined with validation pipes ensure type safety and data integrity.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: response-handling
subtopics.title: Response Handling
subtopics.description: NestJS provides two approaches for handling responses: the standard approach (recommended) where the return value is automatically serialized to JSON, and the library-specific approach using @Res() to access the underlying Express/Fastify response object. Understanding status codes, headers, redirects, and response serialization is key to building proper APIs.
subtopics.content:
# Response Handling

NestJS provides two approaches for handling responses: the standard approach (recommended) where the return value is automatically serialized to JSON, and the library-specific approach using @Res() to access the underlying Express/Fastify response object. Understanding status codes, headers, redirects, and response serialization is key to building proper APIs.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

modules.name: EcMitPZV091OF9Aktmht
modules.title: Validation
modules.description: Input validation is critical for any production API. NestJS provides seamless integration with class-validator and class-transformer libraries, enabling declarative validation using decorators. Combined with the built-in ValidationPipe, NestJS can automatically validate incoming request data against DTO definitions and transform payloads into proper class instances.

subtopics.name: class-validator
subtopics.title: class-validator
subtopics.description: class-validator is a library that allows using decorator-based validation on class properties. Decorators like @IsString(), @IsEmail(), @IsNotEmpty(), @MinLength(), @MaxLength(), @IsEnum(), and many more can be applied to DTO properties. When combined with NestJS's ValidationPipe, invalid requests are automatically rejected with descriptive error messages.
subtopics.content:
# class-validator

class-validator is a library that allows using decorator-based validation on class properties. Decorators like @IsString(), @IsEmail(), @IsNotEmpty(), @MinLength(), @MaxLength(), @IsEnum(), and many more can be applied to DTO properties. When combined with NestJS's ValidationPipe, invalid requests are automatically rejected with descriptive error messages.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Validation](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/validation)

subtopics.name: class-transformer
subtopics.title: class-transformer
subtopics.description: class-transformer is a companion library to class-validator that transforms plain JavaScript objects into class instances and vice versa. It provides decorators like @Exclude(), @Expose(), @Type(), and @Transform() to control serialization/deserialization. In NestJS, it works with the ValidationPipe's transform option to automatically convert request payloads into typed DTO instances.
subtopics.content:
# class-transformer

class-transformer is a companion library to class-validator that transforms plain JavaScript objects into class instances and vice versa. It provides decorators like @Exclude(), @Expose(), @Type(), and @Transform() to control serialization/deserialization. In NestJS, it works with the ValidationPipe's transform option to automatically convert request payloads into typed DTO instances.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Serialization](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/serialization)

subtopics.name: validation-pipe
subtopics.title: ValidationPipe
subtopics.description: The ValidationPipe is a built-in pipe in NestJS that leverages class-validator and class-transformer to validate incoming request data. It can be applied globally, per-controller, or per-route. Options include whitelist (strip non-whitelisted properties), forbidNonWhitelisted (throw on unknown properties), transform (auto-transform payloads), and disableErrorMessages.
subtopics.content:
# ValidationPipe

The ValidationPipe is a built-in pipe in NestJS that leverages class-validator and class-transformer to validate incoming request data. It can be applied globally, per-controller, or per-route. Options include whitelist (strip non-whitelisted properties), forbidNonWhitelisted (throw on unknown properties), transform (auto-transform payloads), and disableErrorMessages.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Validation Pipe](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/validation#using-the-built-in-validationpipe)

modules.title: Database Integration
modules.description: NestJS supports multiple database integration strategies through official packages. TypeORM, Prisma, and Mongoose are the most popular choices. TypeORM provides an Active Record/Data Mapper pattern for SQL databases, Prisma offers a modern type-safe query builder, and Mongoose is the standard ODM for MongoDB. Understanding basic CRUD operations with at least one ORM is essential.

subtopics.name: typeorm-integration
subtopics.title: TypeORM Integration
subtopics.description: TypeORM is the most mature ORM for TypeScript and integrates seamlessly with NestJS via @nestjs/typeorm. It supports Active Record and Data Mapper patterns, decorators for entity definition (@Entity, @Column, @PrimaryGeneratedColumn), and provides repository patterns for CRUD operations. It works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and other SQL databases.
subtopics.content:
# TypeORM Integration

TypeORM is the most mature ORM for TypeScript and integrates seamlessly with NestJS via @nestjs/typeorm. It supports Active Record and Data Mapper patterns, decorators for entity definition (@Entity, @Column, @PrimaryGeneratedColumn), and provides repository patterns for CRUD operations. It works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and other SQL databases.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - TypeORM Integration](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/database)
- [@official@TypeORM Documentation](https://typeorm.io/)
- [@article@NestJS with TypeORM](https://blog.logrocket.com/how-to-build-a-restful-api-with-nestjs/)

- [@video@NestJS TypeORM Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W1gvIw0GNl8)

subtopics.name: prisma-integration
subtopics.title: Prisma Integration
subtopics.description: Prisma is a modern database toolkit that provides a type-safe query builder, automatic migrations, and an intuitive data modeling language. NestJS integrates with Prisma by creating a PrismaService that extends PrismaClient. Prisma's schema-first approach generates a fully typed client, providing excellent TypeScript support and autocompletion.
subtopics.content:
# Prisma Integration

Prisma is a modern database toolkit that provides a type-safe query builder, automatic migrations, and an intuitive data modeling language. NestJS integrates with Prisma by creating a PrismaService that extends PrismaClient. Prisma's schema-first approach generates a fully typed client, providing excellent TypeScript support and autocompletion.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Prisma Recipe](https://docs.nestjs.com/recipes/prisma)

modules.name: aPma34T9jfvypiRT9V21
modules.title: Middleware
modules.description: Middleware is a function that is called before the route handler. Middleware functions have access to the request and response objects, and the next() middleware function. They can execute code, modify request/response objects, end the request-response cycle, or call the next middleware. NestJS supports both class-based and functional middleware.

subtopics.name: creating-middleware
subtopics.title: Creating Middleware
subtopics.description: In NestJS, middleware can be created as a class implementing the NestMiddleware interface with a use() method, or as a simple function. Class-based middleware supports dependency injection, allowing you to inject services. Middleware is registered in a module's configure() method using the MiddlewareConsumer.
subtopics.content:
# Creating Middleware

In NestJS, middleware can be created as a class implementing the NestMiddleware interface with a use() method, or as a simple function. Class-based middleware supports dependency injection, allowing you to inject services. Middleware is registered in a module's configure() method using the MiddlewareConsumer.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Middleware](https://docs.nestjs.com/middleware)
- [@article@Creating Custom Middleware in NestJS](https://www.tomray.dev/nestjs-middleware)

subtopics.name: applying-middleware
subtopics.title: Applying Middleware
subtopics.description: Middleware is applied in the module's configure() method using the MiddlewareConsumer. You can apply middleware to specific routes using forRoutes(), exclude routes with exclude(), and apply multiple middleware in sequence. Middleware can be applied globally using app.use() in the bootstrap function or to specific controllers/routes.
subtopics.content:
# Applying Middleware

Middleware is applied in the module's configure() method using the MiddlewareConsumer. You can apply middleware to specific routes using forRoutes(), exclude routes with exclude(), and apply multiple middleware in sequence. subtopics.name: logging-middleware

modules.title: Guards
modules.description: Guards determine whether a given request will be handled by the route handler, typically used for authentication and authorization. A guard is a class implementing the CanActivate interface with a canActivate() method that returns a boolean. Guards execute after middleware but before interceptors and pipes.

subtopics.name: canactivate-interface
subtopics.title: CanActivate Interface
subtopics.description: The CanActivate interface requires implementing a canActivate() method that receives the ExecutionContext. This method returns a boolean (or Promise<boolean> or Observable<boolean>) indicating whether the request should proceed. The ExecutionContext provides access to the request object, handler metadata, and class reference.
subtopics.content:
# CanActivate Interface

The CanActivate interface requires implementing a canActivate() method that receives the ExecutionContext. This method returns a boolean (or Promise<boolean> or Observable<boolean>) indicating whether the request should proceed. The ExecutionContext provides access to the request object, handler metadata, and class reference.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: auth-guard
subtopics.title: AuthGuard
subtopics.description: AuthGuard is a guard provided by @nestjs/passport that integrates Passport.js strategies with NestJS. It automatically triggers the authentication strategy (JWT, Local, etc.) and attaches the authenticated user to the request object. Custom AuthGuards can extend the built-in AuthGuard to add custom logic like role checking or token refresh.
subtopics.content:
# AuthGuard

AuthGuard is a guard provided by @nestjs/passport that integrates Passport.js strategies with NestJS. It automatically triggers the authentication strategy (JWT, Local, etc.) and attaches the authenticated user to the request object. Custom AuthGuards can extend the built-in AuthGuard to add custom logic like role checking or token refresh.

modules.title: Interceptors and Pipes
modules.description: Interceptors and Pipes are two powerful NestJS features. Pipes transform and validate input data before it reaches the route handler. Interceptors wrap the route handler execution, allowing you to add extra logic before/after handler execution, transform results, extend behavior, and override functions. Both use the @Injectable() decorator and can be scoped globally, per-controller, or per-route.

subtopics.name: custom-pipes
subtopics.title: Custom Pipes
subtopics.description: Custom pipes implement the PipeTransform interface with a transform() method. They receive the input value and metadata (argument type, metatype, data) and return the transformed value. Common use cases include custom validation logic, data type coercion, and business-specific transformations that go beyond what class-validator provides.
subtopics.content:
# Custom Pipes

Custom pipes implement the PipeTransform interface with a transform() method. They receive the input value and metadata (argument type, metatype, data) and return the transformed value. Common use cases include custom validation logic, data type coercion, and business-specific transformations that go beyond what class-validator provides.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: interceptors
subtopics.title: Interceptors
subtopics.description: Interceptors implement the NestInterceptor interface with an intercept() method that receives ExecutionContext and CallHandler. Using RxJS operators on the Observable returned by handle(), interceptors can transform responses (map), handle errors (catchError), add timeout logic, implement caching, and log execution time. They execute in a specific order when multiple are applied.
subtopics.content:
# Interceptors

Interceptors implement the NestInterceptor interface with an intercept() method that receives ExecutionContext and CallHandler. Using RxJS operators on the Observable returned by handle(), interceptors can transform responses (map), handle errors (catchError), add timeout logic, implement caching, and log execution time. They execute in a specific order when multiple are applied.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: response-transformation
subtopics.title: Response Transformation
subtopics.description: Interceptors can transform the response data before it is sent to the client. Common patterns include wrapping responses in a standard format (e.g., { data, meta, status }), removing sensitive fields, converting date formats, or adding pagination metadata. The ClassSerializerInterceptor combined with class-transformer decorators provides a declarative way to control response shape.

modules.name: fO8v38KlmKKgT0ZDi0pt
modules.title: Authentication & Authorization
modules.description: Authentication verifies who the user is, while authorization determines what they can do. NestJS provides robust support for both through Passport.js integration (@nestjs/passport), JWT tokens (@nestjs/jwt), and a Guards-based authorization system. Implementing secure auth flows is critical for any production application.

subtopics.name: jwt-authentication
subtopics.title: JWT Authentication
subtopics.description: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide a stateless authentication mechanism. NestJS's @nestjs/jwt and @nestjs/passport packages work together to implement JWT auth: users log in with credentials, receive a signed token, and include it in subsequent requests via the Authorization header. The JwtStrategy validates and decodes the token on protected routes.
subtopics.content:
# JWT Authentication

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide a stateless authentication mechanism. NestJS's @nestjs/jwt and @nestjs/passport packages work together to implement JWT auth: users log in with credentials, receive a signed token, and include it in subsequent requests via the Authorization header. The JwtStrategy validates and decodes the token on protected routes.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - JWT Authentication](https://docs.nestjs.com/security/authentication#jwt-functionality)

subtopics.name: passport-integration
subtopics.title: Passport.js Integration
subtopics.description: Passport.js is a popular Node.js authentication middleware with 500+ strategies. NestJS integrates Passport through @nestjs/passport, which adapts Passport strategies to work with NestJS's guard system. The LocalStrategy handles username/password authentication, while JwtStrategy handles token-based authentication. Custom strategies can be created by extending PassportStrategy.
subtopics.content:
# Passport.js Integration

Passport.js is a popular Node.js authentication middleware with 500+ strategies. NestJS integrates Passport through @nestjs/passport, which adapts Passport strategies to work with NestJS's guard system. The LocalStrategy handles username/password authentication, while JwtStrategy handles token-based authentication. Custom strategies can be created by extending PassportStrategy.

subtopics.name: role-based-access-control
subtopics.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
subtopics.description: RBAC restricts access to resources based on user roles (e.g., admin, user, moderator). In NestJS, RBAC is implemented using custom decorators (@Roles('admin')), guards (RolesGuard) that read metadata via Reflector, and enum-based role definitions. The guard checks if the authenticated user's role matches the required roles for the route.
subtopics.content:

In NestJS, RBAC is implemented using custom decorators (@Roles('admin')), guards (RolesGuard) that read metadata via Reflector, and enum-based role definitions. The guard checks if the authenticated user's role matches the required roles for the route.

modules.title: Database Mastery
modules.description: Beyond basic CRUD, mastering databases in NestJS involves understanding relational database design, migrations, relationships (One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-Many), query optimization, and transaction management. These skills are essential for building scalable, data-intensive applications.

subtopics.name: relational-database-design
subtopics.title: Relational Database Design
subtopics.description: Designing relational databases involves defining entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them. In NestJS with TypeORM or Prisma, this means creating entity classes or schema models that represent tables, defining primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, and constraints. Understanding normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) helps create efficient, maintainable database schemas.
subtopics.content:
# Relational Database Design

Designing relational databases involves defining entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them. In NestJS with TypeORM or Prisma, this means creating entity classes or schema models that represent tables, defining primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, and constraints. Understanding normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) helps create efficient, maintainable database schemas.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: migrations
subtopics.title: Migrations
subtopics.description: Database migrations are version-controlled changes to the database schema. They allow teams to evolve the database structure over time in a predictable, reproducible way. TypeORM provides a migration CLI and API, Prisma uses 'prisma migrate' for migration management. Understanding how to create, run, and revert migrations is crucial for production deployments.
subtopics.content:

Database migrations are version-controlled changes to the database schema. They allow teams to evolve the database structure over time in a predictable, reproducible way. subtopics.description: Database relationships define how entities relate to each other: One-to-One (user ↔ profile), One-to-Many (user → posts), Many-to-Many (posts ↔ tags). subtopics.content:
# Relationships (OneToMany, ManyToMany)

Database relationships define how entities relate to each other: One-to-One (user ↔ profile), One-to-Many (user → posts), Many-to-Many (posts ↔ tags). In TypeORM, relationships are defined using decorators (@OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @JoinTable). In Prisma, relationships are defined in the schema with relation fields. modules.name: QZa8hDOiHLk2RGME5B1L
modules.title: Error Handling
modules.description: Proper error handling ensures a good developer and user experience. NestJS provides HttpException classes, exception filters, and a built-in exception layer that catches unhandled exceptions. Understanding how to throw appropriate HTTP exceptions, create custom exception filters, and handle errors globally is essential for production-ready APIs.

subtopics.name: http-exceptions
subtopics.title: HttpException
subtopics.description: NestJS provides built-in HTTP exception classes like BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, NotFoundException, ForbiddenException, ConflictException, and InternalServerErrorException. These extend the base HttpException class and automatically set the correct HTTP status code and error format. Custom exception classes can extend HttpException for domain-specific errors.
subtopics.content:
# HttpException

NestJS provides built-in HTTP exception classes like BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, NotFoundException, ForbiddenException, ConflictException, and InternalServerErrorException. These extend the base HttpException class and automatically set the correct HTTP status code and error format. Custom exception classes can extend HttpException for domain-specific errors.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Built-in HTTP Exceptions](https://docs.nestjs.com/exception-filters#built-in-http-exceptions)

subtopics.name: exception-filters
subtopics.title: Exception Filters
subtopics.description: Exception filters provide full control over the exceptions layer. They implement the ExceptionFilter interface with a catch() method that receives the exception and the ArgumentsHost. Filters can be scoped to a single route, controller, or globally. Custom filters allow you to customize error response format, log errors, send alerts, or handle specific exception types differently.
subtopics.content:
# Exception Filters

Exception filters provide full control over the exceptions layer. They implement the ExceptionFilter interface with a catch() method that receives the exception and the ArgumentsHost. Filters can be scoped to a single route, controller, or globally. Custom filters allow you to customize error response format, log errors, send alerts, or handle specific exception types differently.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@article@Custom Exception Filters in NestJS](https://www.tomray.dev/nestjs-exception-filters)

subtopics.name: global-error-handling
subtopics.title: Global Error Handling
subtopics.description: Global error handling ensures all unhandled exceptions in the application are caught and processed consistently. NestJS provides a global exception filter using APP_FILTER or app.useGlobalFilters(). A global filter can standardize error response format, integrate with logging services (Winston, Pino), and provide a fallback for uncaught exceptions across the entire application.
subtopics.content:
# Global Error Handling

Global error handling ensures all unhandled exceptions in the application are caught and processed consistently. NestJS provides a global exception filter using APP_FILTER or app.useGlobalFilters(). A global filter can standardize error response format, integrate with logging services (Winston, Pino), and provide a fallback for uncaught exceptions across the entire application.

modules.description: API documentation is crucial for developer experience and team collaboration. NestJS provides first-class Swagger/OpenAPI integration through @nestjs/swagger. It auto-generates interactive API documentation from your controllers, DTOs, and decorators, allowing developers to test endpoints directly in the browser.

subtopics.name: swagger-setup
subtopics.title: Swagger Setup
subtopics.description: Setting up Swagger in NestJS involves installing @nestjs/swagger and swagger-ui-express, creating a DocumentBuilder to configure API metadata (title, description, version, tags), and calling SwaggerModule.createDocument() and SwaggerModule.setup() in the bootstrap function. The Swagger UI is then accessible at a configured path (e.g., /api).
subtopics.content:
# Swagger Setup

Setting up Swagger in NestJS involves installing @nestjs/swagger and swagger-ui-express, creating a DocumentBuilder to configure API metadata (title, description, version, tags), and calling SwaggerModule.createDocument() and SwaggerModule.setup() in the bootstrap function. The Swagger UI is then accessible at a configured path (e.g., /api).

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - OpenAPI Introduction](https://docs.nestjs.com/openapi/introduction)
- [@article@Setting Up Swagger in NestJS](https://blog.logrocket.com/nestjs-swagger/)

subtopics.name: swagger-decorators
subtopics.title: Swagger Decorators
subtopics.description: NestJS Swagger decorators enhance the auto-generated documentation. @ApiTags() groups endpoints, @ApiOperation() describes the operation, @ApiResponse() documents response types, @ApiProperty() describes DTO properties, @ApiBearerAuth() adds JWT auth, and @ApiQuery()/@ApiParam() document parameters. The CLI plugin can automatically apply decorators based on DTOs.
subtopics.content:
# Swagger Decorators

NestJS Swagger decorators enhance the auto-generated documentation. @ApiTags() groups endpoints, @ApiOperation() describes the operation, @ApiResponse() documents response types, @ApiProperty() describes DTO properties, @ApiBearerAuth() adds JWT auth, and @ApiQuery()/@ApiParam() document parameters. modules.name: guAYALttJPFlXH1kDi_t
modules.title: Testing
modules.description: Testing is a critical part of building reliable NestJS applications. NestJS provides excellent testing utilities through @nestjs/testing, which creates a testing module that mirrors the application's dependency injection system. Jest is the default test runner, and NestJS supports both unit testing (services, controllers) and end-to-end testing.

subtopics.name: jest-setup
subtopics.title: Jest Setup & Configuration
subtopics.description: NestJS projects come pre-configured with Jest. The jest configuration in package.json or jest.config.ts includes TypeScript support via ts-jest, module path mapping, coverage configuration, and test file patterns (.spec.ts). Understanding Jest's matcher API (expect, toBe, toEqual, toHaveBeenCalled) and async testing patterns (async/await, done callback) is essential.
subtopics.content:
# Jest Setup & Configuration

NestJS projects come pre-configured with Jest. The jest configuration in package.json or jest.config.ts includes TypeScript support via ts-jest, module path mapping, coverage configuration, and test file patterns (.spec.ts). Understanding Jest's matcher API (expect, toBe, toEqual, toHaveBeenCalled) and async testing patterns (async/await, done callback) is essential.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: unit-testing-services
subtopics.title: Unit Testing Services
subtopics.description: Unit testing services involves creating a testing module with Test.createTestingModule(), mocking dependencies (repositories, external services), and testing each method in isolation. Mocking is done using Jest's jest.fn(), jest.spyOn(), or custom mock factories. The goal is to verify business logic without database calls or HTTP requests.
subtopics.content:
# Unit Testing Services

Unit testing services involves creating a testing module with Test.createTestingModule(), mocking dependencies (repositories, external services), and testing each method in isolation. Mocking is done using Jest's jest.fn(), jest.spyOn(), or custom mock factories. The goal is to verify business logic without database calls or HTTP requests.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: unit-testing-controllers

modules.title: Microservices Architecture
modules.description: NestJS provides a built-in microservices package (@nestjs/microservices) that supports multiple transport layers. subtopics.name: nestjs-microservices-basics

subtopics.description: The @nestjs/microservices package provides the foundation for building microservices with NestJS. It introduces concepts like transport layers, message patterns (@MessagePattern), event patterns (@EventPattern), and the ClientProxy for inter-service communication. subtopics.content:

NestJS integrates with RabbitMQ through the @nestjs/microservices package, enabling reliable message delivery with features like message acknowledgment, dead-letter queues, message persistence, and exchange routing. It's ideal for task queues, event broadcasting, and reliable async processing.

subtopics.name: kafka-transport

modules.name: uhCNo2LHJuihkrhDcIBa
modules.title: Advanced Authentication
modules.description: Beyond basic JWT authentication, advanced auth scenarios include OAuth2/OpenID Connect integration, Single Sign-On (SSO), social login (Google, GitHub, Facebook), and multi-factor authentication. NestJS supports these through Passport strategies and dedicated packages.

subtopics.name: oauth2-sso

subtopics.description: OAuth2 is an authorization framework that enables applications to obtain limited access to user accounts on third-party services. Single Sign-On (SSO) allows users to authenticate once and access multiple services. NestJS supports OAuth2 flows (Authorization Code, Client Credentials) through Passport strategies and dedicated OAuth2 libraries.

OAuth2 is an authorization framework that enables applications to obtain limited access to user accounts on third-party services. subtopics.name: passport-strategies

modules.title: Caching & Performance
modules.description: Performance optimization is critical for production applications. NestJS provides built-in caching mechanisms through @nestjs/cache-manager, supporting multiple stores including in-memory and Redis. Understanding caching strategies, query optimization, and response compression helps build high-performance APIs.

subtopics.name: redis-caching
subtopics.title: Redis Caching
subtopics.description: Redis is the most popular caching solution for NestJS applications. Using @nestjs/cache-manager with the cache-manager-redis-store, you can cache API responses, database queries, and computed results. Redis caching supports TTL (Time-to-Live), cache invalidation, and distributed caching across multiple application instances.
subtopics.content:
# Redis Caching

Redis is the most popular caching solution for NestJS applications. Using @nestjs/cache-manager with the cache-manager-redis-store, you can cache API responses, database queries, and computed results. Redis caching supports TTL (Time-to-Live), cache invalidation, and distributed caching across multiple application instances.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

- [@official@NestJS - Caching](https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/caching)
- [@article@Redis Caching in NestJS](https://blog.logrocket.com/nestjs-caching-redis/)

subtopics.name: in-memory-cache
subtopics.title: In-Memory Cache
subtopics.description: NestJS's built-in cache manager defaults to an in-memory store. It's useful for single-instance applications and development. Using the @CacheKey() and @CacheTTL() decorators with the CacheInterceptor, responses can be cached at the controller or route level. In-memory caching is the simplest approach but doesn't persist across restarts or scale across instances.
subtopics.content:

In-memory caching is the simplest approach but doesn't persist across restarts or scale across instances.

subtopics.name: query-optimization
subtopics.title: Query Optimization
subtopics.description: Query optimization involves reducing database load and improving response times. Key techniques include: selecting only needed columns, proper indexing, eager/lazy loading strategies, pagination (offset-based and cursor-based), query caching, avoiding N+1 queries with join strategies, and using raw queries for complex operations. Both TypeORM and Prisma provide tools for query analysis and optimization.

modules.name: BEgbEiJnxGU4Yqi-HMfg
modules.title: WebSockets & Real-Time
modules.description: NestJS provides built-in support for WebSockets through @nestjs/websockets and @nestjs/platform-socket.io (or @nestjs/platform-ws). subtopics.name: websocket-gateway
subtopics.title: WebSocket Gateway
subtopics.description: A WebSocket Gateway is a class decorated with @WebSocketGateway() that handles WebSocket connections. It uses @SubscribeMessage() to listen for events, @WebSocketServer() to access the server instance, and lifecycle hooks (OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect) to manage connection lifecycle. Gateways support namespaces, rooms, and middleware.
subtopics.content:
# WebSocket Gateway

A WebSocket Gateway is a class decorated with @WebSocketGateway() that handles WebSocket connections. It uses @SubscribeMessage() to listen for events, @WebSocketServer() to access the server instance, and lifecycle hooks (OnGatewayInit, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect) to manage connection lifecycle. Gateways support namespaces, rooms, and middleware.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: real-time-events

subtopics.name: docker-containerization

subtopics.name: cqrs-pattern
subtopics.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
subtopics.description: CQRS separates read and write operations into different models. NestJS provides the @nestjs/cqrs package with built-in support for commands, queries, events, and sagas. Commands modify state (CreateUserCommand), queries read state (GetUserQuery), and events notify about state changes (UserCreatedEvent). This pattern improves scalability by allowing independent optimization of read and write paths.
subtopics.content:
# CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

CQRS separates read and write operations into different models. NestJS provides the @nestjs/cqrs package with built-in support for commands, queries, events, and sagas. Commands modify state (CreateUserCommand), queries read state (GetUserQuery), and events notify about state changes (UserCreatedEvent). This pattern improves scalability by allowing independent optimization of read and write paths.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.content:
# Event Sourcing

Event Sourcing stores the state of an application as a sequence of events rather than the current state. Each event represents a change that happened, and the current state is reconstructed by replaying events. Combined with CQRS, event sourcing provides a complete audit trail, temporal queries, and the ability to rebuild state. NestJS's @nestjs/cqrs package provides event bus and event handler infrastructure.

modules.description: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) is a design pattern where systems communicate through the production, detection, and consumption of events. subtopics.name: event-emitter
subtopics.title: Event Emitter (@nestjs/event-emitter)
subtopics.description: The @nestjs/event-emitter package provides a local event system for NestJS applications using the eventemitter2 library. It allows emitting and listening for events within a single application instance. Events are dispatched using EventEmitter2.emit() and handled by methods decorated with @OnEvent(). This is useful for decoupling modules without the overhead of an external message broker.
subtopics.content:
# Event Emitter (@nestjs/event-emitter)

The @nestjs/event-emitter package provides a local event system for NestJS applications using the eventemitter2 library. It allows emitting and listening for events within a single application instance. Events are dispatched using EventEmitter2.emit() and handled by methods decorated with @OnEvent(). This is useful for decoupling modules without the overhead of an external message broker.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: message-brokers
subtopics.title: Message Brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)
subtopics.description: External message brokers enable asynchronous communication between distributed services. Kafka excels at high-throughput event streaming, RabbitMQ provides flexible routing and reliable delivery, and AWS SQS offers managed queue services. Each broker has different guarantees (at-least-once, at-most-once, exactly-once) and use cases. Choosing the right broker depends on throughput, ordering, and durability requirements.
subtopics.content:
# Message Brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)

External message brokers enable asynchronous communication between distributed services. Kafka excels at high-throughput event streaming, RabbitMQ provides flexible routing and reliable delivery, and AWS SQS offers managed queue services. Each broker has different guarantees (at-least-once, at-most-once, exactly-once) and use cases. Choosing the right broker depends on throughput, ordering, and durability requirements.

subtopics.name: rate-limiting

subtopics.description: Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse by restricting the number of requests a client can make within a time window. NestJS provides @nestjs/throttler for rate limiting with configurable TTL and limit values. It supports per-route, per-controller, or global rate limiting, and can be customized for different user roles or API tiers.
subtopics.content:
# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse by restricting the number of requests a client can make within a time window. NestJS provides @nestjs/throttler for rate limiting with configurable TTL and limit values. It supports per-route, per-controller, or global rate limiting, and can be customized for different user roles or API tiers.

Visit the following resources to learn more:

subtopics.name: csrf-protection
subtopics.title: CSRF & XSS Protection
subtopics.description: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) are common web vulnerabilities. NestJS addresses CSRF through csurf middleware for session-based apps, and uses helmet to set security HTTP headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-XSS-Protection, X-Frame-Options). Input sanitization and output encoding prevent XSS attacks.
subtopics.content:
# CSRF & XSS Protection

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) are common web vulnerabilities. NestJS addresses CSRF through csurf middleware for session-based apps, and uses helmet to set security HTTP headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-XSS-Protection, X-Frame-Options). Input sanitization and output encoding prevent XSS attacks.
